diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: I want to tell you a story about a 19th-century chemistry professor who had a unique way of teaching. He showed his students a vial of disgusting liquid and told them a chemist needs two things: a sense of observation and a sense of taste.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: He dipped his finger into the liquid, put it in his mouth, and passed it around. After the students did the same, he said, 'If you had a sense of observation, you'd have noticed I dipped one finger but tasted another.' He was teaching them the danger of not noticing details.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: As humans, we get used to things quickly through a process called habituation. It's how we learn to stop noticing everyday things so we can focus on new ones. While essential for survival and efficiency, like learning to drive, habituation is the enemy for designers.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: Our job is to notice 'invisible' problems that others have learned to live with. Take the sticker on a piece of fruit; we've habituated to the struggle of peeling it and the sticky residue it leaves behind. The first secret of design is noticing—seeing the world as it is, not as we've accepted it.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: When we designed the Nest thermostat, we saw that people had habituated to complex, confusing interfaces they hated but accepted as the norm. To innovate, we had to break that habituation. I have three tips for how to keep noticing: Look broader, look closer, and think younger.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: First, look broader. The problem often isn't the product itself, but the steps leading up to it. By looking at the whole customer journey—the 'before' and 'after'—we improved the iPod experience by ensuring users could play music immediately after unboxing it.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: Second, look closer. Focus on the tiny details that seem insignificant. These small frictions are signs of larger issues. By fixing a dozen tiny details that everyone else ignores, you can create a product that feels intuitive and truly solves the user's hidden problems.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: Third, think younger. Children have a beginner's mind and haven't habituated yet, so they ask 'Why?' constantly. As we grow up, we stop questioning things. To be a great designer, you need to regain that perspective and challenge the assumptions adults take for granted.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: By following these steps, you can see the world with fresh eyes. Don't ignore small frustrations; notice them and use them as opportunities for innovation. It's about fighting habituation every day to create meaningful change and improve the human experience. Thank you.

diarization.speaker: Speaker 2
diarization.text: Tony, that was wonderful. One question: You mentioned looking at the world like a child. Is that a skill that can be taught to a team, or is it just something certain people are born with?

diarization.speaker: Speaker 1
diarization.text: I believe it's a muscle you have to exercise. You must force your team to ask 'why' questions every day and create a culture where 'that's how it's always been' is not an acceptable answer. You have to actively fight the comfort of the familiar to keep innovating.
